Watched, Threatened, Disconnected: Journalists on Digital Frontlines

title: Web3Privacy Now opening speech
Lethe Machina: Privacy When Nothing Fades
description: Privacy engineering governs disclosure; it is far weaker at governing what follows, when traces remain searchable, inferable, executable, and reusable. Drawing on philosophies of memory, oblivion, and the archive, Lethe Machina treats blockchain as both cemetery and temple: an ossuary of active decisions and a programmable space for dormancy, closure, and release. It introduces Lethean gradients—fading, sealing, contextual expiry, and bounded influence—and translates them into a Lethean Readiness Framework for testing whether systems can bind traces to context, let their force decay, make reactivation accountable, and govern what survives deletion. Can privacy preserve evidence without allowing the past to govern indefinitely?
descriptionFull: Cypherpunk privacy has largely been organised around disclosure, secrecy, and control. The Sapphirepunk Manifesto reframed privacy as a condition of relation. Lethe Machina adds the temporal question of how long past relations and traces should retain power. Drawing on Ricœur’s philosophy of forgetting, Stiegler’s tertiary retention, Ernst and Chun’s computational temporality, Derrida’s archive, and Mbembe’s necropolitics, the talk describes digital memory as a loss of thresholds between the active, archival, dormant, and socially finished.

title: Why technology fails us
What does Web3 Privacy mean in an agentic world?
descriptionFull:
Ethereum privacy requires more than hiding a transaction’s contents. The infrastructure must also protect what users read—balances, addresses, contracts—and prevent their network identity from being linked to those requests or their transaction submissions. This talk explores how private reads, privacy-preserving transaction submission, and a distributed network of independent node operators can make privacy part of everyday wallet UX.

Then we extend that foundation to AI agents. If an agent exposes your intent while reasoning, querying data, or building a transaction, a private wallet cannot undo the leak. How can we preserve privacy throughout that process while enforcing explicit security checks before signing? From wallets to agents, we explore what it takes to make private UX future-proof

title: You can't trust your VPN
description: Why conventional VPNs fail to separate your identity from your online activity, and how decentralized VPNs or mixnets could fulfil that promise.
descriptionFull:
VPNs are built on the promise that you can break the link between who you are (your IP) and what you're doing (your online activity). This is fundamental to online privacy, and over a billion users pay $70bn annually for these services. There's just one problem: no legacy VPN can keep this promise. In fact, most make the situation worse.

This talk will explain why that matters, how decentralized VPNs or mixnets can finally live up to the promise, and why everyone can benefit from a web3 approach: users, builders and even regulators.

title: Protecting the Tools that Protect Our Rights
description: When society at large can't or won't stop the spread of ubiquitous surveillance, we need strong privacy technologies that return control and autonomy to users. Yet some of these tools, and the people who build and run them, have come under legal attack. Come learn about these legal threats and how to protect our right to build the tools we need, by practical steps and by working together to create the legal policy space necessary for a free society.

description: Two escapes, one problem: Bob Summerwill shares his ongoing escape from Google and AI, with practical steps to start your own escape tonight.

Two escapes, one problem.
Escape #1, Google.
Escape #2, the AI.

title: The Winners and Losers of the AI Race: A View from the Stack
description: Isha Suri examines power and dependency across the AI stack, and whether open-source AI, local models and alternative cloud infrastructure can redistribute power.
descriptionFull: Isha Suri examines the political economy of AI infrastructure: where power accumulates across the stack, how dependencies are created and reinforced, and what this means for building alternatives. Drawing on research into cloud infrastructure and AI market power, she explores cloud credits, partnerships, switching costs and vertical integration. The talk considers open-source and local AI, open cloud infrastructure, public or shared compute, and different models of ownership and governance, asking whether these alternatives can redistribute power when the underlying infrastructure remains concentrated.

description: There is no excuse anymore: FOSS alternatives are not just more private and secure but also becoming more practical than their proprietary counterparts. Come to discuss alternative apps, operating systems, open hardware and all your tips on how to live on a Free software only diet!
descriptionFull: There is no excuse anymore: FOSS alternatives are not just more private and secure but also becoming more practical than their proprietary counterparts. title: Post Quantum Cryptography: reality check in 2026
description: Cryptography heavyweight will disscuss the state of cryptography in 2026
descriptionFull: There's a lot of panic within cryptography scene: will AI break reliable cryptographic schemas? How far we are before Post-Quantum computers will break everything. Myths vs Practical cryptographic knowledge.

title: Post-quantum collaboration
description: The basics of post-quantum cryptography and how it applies to privacy and security in collaborative files and apps.
descriptionFull: End-to-end encryption (e2ee) gave us a way to gain privacy and security in online collaboration even while most of us were dependent on centralized third parties for these same activities. While e2ee remains far from ubiquitous, the privacy & security frontier has yet again moved due to quantum computers, and it carries with it the same issues that e2ee had: complexity. This talk will cover some of the basics of post-quantum cryptography and how we apply it to Multiplayer Collaboration files & apps. Post Quantum Collaboration is a made-up concept that we'll be unveiling in a light way in Nov with peers, anons, and friends :))

title: Reimagining AI to address the harms inherent in its design
description: Panel will feature academic and practicing experts who are working on evaluating AI models and making them safer. The panel will discuss the specific ways in which the development of foundational AI models is leading to repetitive instances of harms such as NCII, misinformation, etc. Secondly, we will share some broad prescriptions for how these harms can be addressed in the short term and how AI systems must be redesigned to prevent these harms from proliferating.

title: Who Protects Us Online? Cybercrime, Digital Rights and the Fight for a Free and Secure Internet in India.
description: As cyber scams cross messaging platforms, websites, banks and payment systems, victims face fragmented reporting, investigation and recovery processes. This panel examines how India can improve accountability and access to remedies while protecting encryption and digital rights, drawing the boundaries of legitimate surveillance, and making secure tools accessible to everyone.
descriptionFull: As cyber scams cross messaging platforms, websites, banks and payment systems, victims face fragmented reporting, investigation and recovery processes. title: Cypher Atlas, map of the cypherpunk movement
description: Cypher Atlas maps the cypherpunk ecosystem using public sources, helping engineers, lawyers, researchers and communities find one another, understand their connections and make the movement easier to enter.
descriptionFull:
Most of the people this movement needs have never heard the word cypherpunk.

How do they get in? It is a question the movement does not ask itself.

Engineers, lawyers, researchers solving the same problems under different names. Right now you find this movement by accident: the right podcast, the right person, the right conference.

The people already inside cannot see each other either. Five projects solve the same problem. One law takes all five, and they find out separately.

Cypher Atlas is a map of this ecosystem: who is here, what came out of what, and what is coming at it. Built entirely from public sources.

This movement built doors. All of them open from the inside. What happens when a movement that spent fifty years building tools for autonomy finally becomes easier to find, understand and enter?

title: Cypherpunk or Junk: Grading Ethereum's Roadmap
description: Thomas Thiery, Sebastian Bürgel, jimjim and cheeky-gorilla put Ethereum's roadmap on trial: which upgrades put more power in your hands?
descriptionFull:
There's a lot of talk in Ethereum-land about being cypherpunk, but does the roadmap actually reflect those values?

Join Thomas Thiery (Ethereum Foundation), Sebastian Bürgel (Gnosis / HOPR), jimjim (Warptoad) and cheeky-gorilla (Protocol Guild, moderator) as they put the roadmap on trial and judge the upgrades by how cypherpunk they are. Which ones put more power in your hands, and which ones put it in someone else's?

Expect stubborn realism, hard tradeoffs, and no hand-waving. Zero technical knowledge required!

title: Feeding the Cloud: Data centers, knowledge and resistance in India
description: Panel with gather activists that led mass mobilisation of people, award-winning investigative journalists, researchers and advocates of people-centric AI.

title: What it’s like to build products with cypherpunk principles
description: In this talk I’ll cover the tradeoffs that come with building software that allows users to operate in a more secure, private, and self sovereign way. I’ll share my learnings and principles I use from working on the security, privacy, and Web3 teams at Brave browser so you too can help get cypherpunk software into the hands of more users.
descriptionFull:
In this talk, I'll cover in greater depth what I scratched the surface on in this blog post: https://kyledenhartog.com/recreating-web3-cross-origin-tracking/

Come learn some of the ways wallets are reintroducing privacy problems that we've been spending years to fix in Web2 by improving the browser privacy model. As of today Web3 is on track to make the Web privacy model worse as we share our addresses with every new site we visit. This will only get worse as we work to unify chains and make the UX more seamless with Web3 domains turning our wallet addresses into our globally unique third party cookie.

After defining the problem, I'll cover some techniques and principles we can use to redefine how wallets interact with sites and how we as developers can think differently about this problem and propagate it throughout the protocol, sites, and wallets that we're adding to Web2.

AR glasses with a camera and an automated workflow let a stranger learn everything about you in seconds, enough to fake trust and socially engineer you on the spot. DeFi learned to price collateral without trusting people. Now that the attention economy is turning into a trust economy, can we price trust without exploiting it?

title: Governing for baselines | The material foundations of artificial intelligence supply chains
description: Researchers and investigators examine the labour, data centres, and concentrated chip-and-cloud markets behind AI, and the need to engage with the political economy of the full stack.
descriptionFull: Stepping away from the mainstream focus on AI redlines, both real and existential, this panel will instead deal with the very real supply chains that make up the 'AI' we know of and have come to use. From precarious labor that goes into training, curating, and using frontier models, to the resource-intensive data centers facing fierce pushback across the world, all the way to the concentrated chip-and-cloud markets, the AI supply chain shows how this intelligence is anything but artificial. In this panel, researchers and investigators across domains will present findings that reiterate this reality and establish the need to engage with the political economy of AI on multiple levels of the 'stack'.

title: The State Of Ethereum Privacy
Against the criminalization of software development
description: Michael Lewellen shares his lawsuit against the DOJ over the criminalization of software development, and why this fight matters for privacy and free expression. He’ll outline how cypherpunks can defend crypto freedoms and engage in local policy activism.
descriptionFull: Michael Lewellen will discuss his lawsuit challenging the DOJ’s attempt to criminalize open-source software, a case with major implications for developers and privacy advocates. He’ll connect this battle to broader cypherpunk principles—free speech, code as expression, and resistance to surveillance—while offering concrete steps for activists to influence policy and protect crypto freedoms in their communities.

title: More Like Ethereum, Less Like SaaS: Why Businesses Need Cypherpunk Systems
description:
Cypherpunk guarantees are valuable not because everyone wants to live a cypherpunk life, but because credible exit changes the behaviour of the systems people normally use. As businesses move payroll, treasury and payments on-chain, those guarantees become practical requirements. What happens when governance is captured, the founding team disappears, or an intermediary stops cooperating?

Privacy makes the problem concrete. The assets in a system can be recoverable, while losing the privacy that justified using it. Business infrastructure should inherit Ethereum’s trust model rather than recreate vendor dependence one layer higher, and infrastructure built this way benefits everyone.
descriptionFull:
Ethereum offers a unique value proposition: infrastructure with guarantees independent from counterparties. Ethereum works predictably, without the need for a vendor to operate, cooperate, or remain benevolent. But apps built on Ethereum often reintroduce those dependencies one layer higher (eg. governance, upgrade authority, relayers, hosted infra).

For orgs, this is different from an ideological problem. A competitor gaining influence over critical payment infra is counterparty risk. A maintainer team disappearing is continuity risk. An intermediary refusing service is operational risk.

We can use the walkaway test to evaluate what should still work when these dependencies fail. And recovering funds is table stakes. A shielded system can ensure asset recovery while losing the privacy that made it useful.

Business adoption does not require weakening cypherpunk guarantees. In fact, with enough economic importance, I think cypherpunk guarantees will become ordinary infrastructure requirements. We are building systems strong enough for businesses to depend on so that everyone can inherit the same protections.

description: Learn about Zcash, where we are now and where we are headed.

title: Lessons learned from 20 years of Tor
Cypherpunk Silicon [update]
Beyond GitHub: Building Open Source on Radicle
description: Discover how Radicle provides a sovereign, peer-to-peer home for open source. You'll leave knowing how Radicle works, why it matters, why communities choose it over centralized forges and how to start using it.
descriptionFull:
2026 is shaping up to be a turning point for code collaboration. As centralized forges struggle under the growing demands of agentic development, more developers are looking beyond the platform model searching for resilience, ownership, and autonomy.

Radicle has emerged as the most widely used decentralized alternative: a sovereign, p2p network for code collaboration built on Git, with more than 20,000 repositories actively hosted across the network.

In this workshop, we'll introduce Radicle as a permanent home for open source, not only for human developers, but for a new generation of autonomous software agents that need to discover repositories, propose changes and collaborate without relying on a centralized intermediary.

We'll explore how Radicle works, how developers collaborate on repositories, and what peer-to-peer code infrastructure makes possible for human and agentic workflows.

Come with a laptop and Radicle installed.

title: Intersection of local-first, privacy and web3 with Logos
description: In this talk, we explore why local-first software, privacy and web3 are stronger together than apart. Local-first puts data back in the user's custody, privacy keeps it out of reach of surveillance and web3 removes the central servers that can censor or shut you down.

description: Today, a few large corporations like Palantir are using AI as a mass surveillance machine to create a perfectly controllable 'digital twin' of reality. Learning from cypherpunk history and our own recent lessons building NymVPN, we will sketch an alternative vision for anonymity and freedom beyond blockchains.

title: After Encryption
description: The widespread application of encryption and privacy tools to security-critical applications has created a world where governments have started targeting the use of these tools instead of the content of the tools. To respond to this we need to imagine new forms of security. I propose one such tool in the form of textual stenography which allows you to use encryption while appearing to post normal encrypted text.

title: LeakDetect: Measuring Privacy Leakage in Web3 Wallets, Agents and P2P networks
description:
Privacy-preserving cryptography can protect what is written to a blockchain, but it cannot necessarily protect everything that happens around it. Wallets, applications, P2P networks and autonomous agents continuously generate observable signals that may reveal information through timing, behavior, metadata, execution patterns and communication.

LeakDetect explores this broader privacy problem across Ethereum and privacy-focused systems including Zcash and Tornado Cash, asking a simple but fundamental cypherpunk question: what can an observer infer when the cryptography is working as intended?

In this 30-minute talk, we will examine how information leakage can emerge across wallets, transactions, network interactions and emerging agentic systems. We will introduce an observability-driven approach to identifying and measuring these signals, including adversarial experimentation, inference techniques and quantitative approaches to privacy leakage.

The talk will explore how individually innocuous signals can become privacy-sensitive when correlated, and how the rise of autonomous agents introduces new behavioral and communication surfaces that may require entirely new privacy threat models.

Rather than treating privacy as binary, LeakDetect asks us to measure privacy under realistic observation:
What does the system reveal, to whom, under which observations, and how much can be inferred?

We will conclude with open research questions and opportunities for building privacy-preserving wallets, agents and decentralized infrastructure that remain resilient not only to direct attacks, but also to observation, inference and surveillance.
descriptionFull:
LeakDetect investigates a fundamental cypherpunk question: what can privacy-preserving systems reveal even when their underlying cryptography is working as intended?

The project focuses on information leakage across Ethereum, Zcash and Tornado Cash, examining not only protocols and transactions, but also the surrounding layers where privacy can unintentionally break down.
Our research explores leakage in wallets, P2P communication, transaction behaviour, timing, network metadata, RPC/API interactions and autonomous agents. For AI and agentic systems, we are particularly interested in whether an agent’s actions, execution patterns or communication behavior can expose information about users, strategies, identities or intent.

Using adversarial simulation, observability and machine-learning-assisted inference, LeakDetect aims to identify signals that can be correlated to reconstruct information that users may reasonably expect to remain private.

The research asks:
What does a privacy-preserving system reveal to an observer, and how much can be inferred from those signals?

Rather than assuming privacy is binary, we want to measure leakage quantitatively across different threat models and layers.

The work will explore reproducible experiments and open benchmarks for comparing privacy leakage across Ethereum and privacy-focused ecosystems such as Zcash and Tornado Cash, while examining the role of wallets and emerging autonomous agents as new privacy attack surfaces.

The goal is to develop open research tooling, datasets, benchmarks and methodologies that enable privacy researchers, cryptographers, security practitioners and protocol developers to identify and reduce unintended information leakage.

Ultimately, LeakDetect moves the conversation from:
“Is cryptography private?”
to:
“Is the entire system, including its wallets, agents, network and observable behaviour, private under realistic observation?”

title: Privacy on Chain: What Stealth Addresses Solve
description: A practical walkthrough of stealth addresses, ERC-5564 and real-world engineering hurdles, followed by a look at how zero-knowledge proofs and Keystore architectures could improve key rotation and user experience.
descriptionFull: A practical, workshop-style technical walkthrough of how stealth addresses work under the hood. We'll break down the cryptographic flow, modern standards like ERC-5564, and the real-world engineering hurdles (fragmentation, UTXO-like selection). We will also look ahead at the future of onchain privacy, exploring how Zero-Knowledge Proofs and Keystore architectures are set to solve key rotation and improve UX, transforming fragmented addresses into a seamless, automated privacy layer for organizations and individuals alike.

title: Reimagining social media from the margins
description: In reclaiming social media, we reclaim possibilities, voice, and agency.
descriptionFull: In 2025, Point of View in collaboration with Quicksand organised multi-city consultations across India — Goa, Bangalore, Mumbai, Delhi, and Hyderabad — with women, gender-diverse people, sex workers, people with disabilities, designers, technologists, and researchers to reimagine social media. Riddhima Sharma will share results of this work & vision how social media can be places of care, safe by design, and value-based.

title: Wilderness and Privacy: When Cybersecurity Fails
description: Until now, humans have been protected by civilized society and allowed to exercise their social skills without feeling any personal danger. However, the deterioration of cybersecurity and the increasing sophistication of crime through AI are destroying that premise. Just as wild animals live by holding their breath and emitting no signals, humans will be forced to live while concealing much of their information. I will discuss what privacy is needed in an era of regression to an advanced wilderness.

title: Mother of All VPNs: The First 9 Months
description: Started as a response to the frustration and rage following the massacre in Iran and the internet shutdowns in January 2026. A crazy idea that, once put together, actually started to work. Not just in Iran, but in Myanmar, Russia, and elsewhere. First presented at the Neo-Cypherpunk Congress in Berlin, followed by DappCon. Both were turning points in realizing I might actually be onto something. A full-on developer mode over the summer, building, breaking, fixing, and experimenting. At the Global Gathering summit, seeing people from Tor, OONI, and others so excited to hear more about MoaV was another big moment. Basically, this talk is about the birth and rise of MoaV. The story behind it, what worked, what didn’t, how it’s going, and how I envision it growing from here.

title: Privacy Activism, Privacy Wars, Network States (With A Privacy Focus)
description: ENS is detecting a surge of DNS hijacks targeting Web3, exploiting centralized DNS to steal keys and drain wallets. This talk flips the script—showing how reclaiming hijacked domains can turn them into cypherpunk intelligence hubs that map attacker infrastructure, harvest metadata, and expose threat networks. By weaponizing their own tactics against them, we can harden Ethereum’s naming layer into a censorship‑resistant, privacy‑first system—and take the fight to the root.
descriptionFull: Hijacking the Hijackers: Cypherpunk Tactics for a Safer Ethereum. The Ethereum Name Service (ENS) has been witnessing a staggering rise in DNS-based attacks targeting Web3 users, revealing a critical security and trust gap that threatens Ethereum's open and permissionless future. These attacks, primarily conducted via DNS hijacking and registrar-level compromises, redirect unsuspecting users to malicious sites designed to steal keys and drain wallets—undermining trust, safety, and onboarding efforts for the Ethereum ecosystem. This talk will first unpack the scale and sophistication of these DNS attacks against Web3 entities as detected and mitigated by ENS, highlighting the precarious reliance on centralized Web2 DNS infrastructure that attackers exploit to bypass decentralized protocol security. The resulting damage goes beyond stolen assets; it erodes user confidence, slows mainstream adoption, and endangers Ethereum's promise of inclusivity and sovereignty. I plan on covering the following: Why there is a Massive DNS Attack Wave – ENS is detecting a sharp rise in DNS hijacks and registrar-level compromises that specifically target Web3 users and assets. Exploiting Centralization – Attackers bypass Web3’s cryptographic security by exploiting weak points in centralized Web2 DNS infrastructure. Impact on Ethereum’s Future – These attacks steal funds, erode user trust, and slow onboarding—threatening Ethereum’s promise of openness, safety, and inclusivity. The Cypherpunk Response – Don’t just defend—seize back compromised domains and turn them into assets for the community. Reclaimed Domains as Intel Hubs – Use them as honeypots to collect attacker metadata, trace tactics, and map malicious networks. Turning the Tables – Apply the adversary’s own tools—surveillance & control—against them, in defense of user sovereignty. And I will end with a call to action that involves working with SEAL to develop proactive resilience and why the Ethereum ecosystem must make the DNS into a censorship-resistant, attack-aware, namespace guided by cypherpunk principles of privacy and decentralization.

title: Terminal Values
description: What values do we uphold as cypherpunks in 2026? Lessons from a long-lasting activist
descriptionFull: Danny spent decade in Electronic Frontier Foundation as an activist, international director, and finally, director of strategy. He was around the first-wave of cypherpunks, seen creation of cryptographic activism. Now it's time to share his vision on cypherpunk values that will work in 2026

title: Why Every Supply Chain Blockchain Died: Capture, Neutrality, and Lessons from Inside
description: Tradelens, Food Trust, TRACR, Provenance, Skuchain, Open SC: a decade of well-funded supply chain blockchains, and no blockchain success stories. Having architected and consulted two of them, I dissect the shared failure modes — capture by middlemen, missing neutrality, blockchain-as-database — and derive design principles for trade infrastructure that can actually survive and have lasting, positive impact on painful real world challenges.
descriptionFull: Supply chain tracing is the use case blockchain was seemingly made for, yet every major attempt collapsed or quietly dropped the chain. This is a structured post-mortem from unusual proximity: I was IBM's first blockchain architect in the Hyperledger and Tradelens era, and architected De Beers' TRACR at BCG. Across six case studies I extract a failure taxonomy: systems deployed BY the intermediaries they should have disintermediated (capture), sponsors unable to be credibly neutral (Tradelens' unresolvable problem), tokenless designs that reduced the chain to an expensive database, and exclusion of the small producers who needed the system most. From the failures I derive testable design principles for capture-resistant trade infrastructure: credible neutrality, full use of the transactional stack, SME-first economics, and readable contracts — and show how they hold up in a live open-infrastructure experiment in fresh food. Attendees leave with the checklist I wish I'd had.

title: Closing ceremony with digital rights & FOSS advocates
